Seatback frame design evolution through multiple iterations to improve mechanical performance while decreasing weight. The design 1 shown in Fig. 4.2.2 consists of some of the original parts from the Ford’s design while the rest of the polymer composite parts are designed to fit with the metal parts enabling the lightweight for the seatback frame. The detailed labelling of various parts for design 2 is shown in Fig. 4.2.3. (a). The von mises stress and displacement contours for the design 1 are illustrated in Fig. 4.2.3 (b) & (c), respectively. Although the design is lightweight, the deformation is significantly higher along with the max. stress. Thus, the design 1 needs to modified to make it stiffer. The preliminary design 1 is improved in the polymer composite frame to enable it to be structurally stiffer as shown in design 2. The detailed labelling of various parts for design 2 is shown in Fig. 4.2.4. (a). The von mises stress and displacement contours for the design 2 are illustrated in Fig. 4.2.4 (b) & (c), respectively. The seat bracket attachment location for the polymer composite frame on the left-hand side 19 | P age caused a high stress concentration location and thus requires further modification as shown in design 3. A schematic diagram of design 3 is shown in Fig. 4.4.4. The polymer composite frame on the left side of seatback is optimally designed to take the load while ensuring the weight is minimal. The von mises stress, strain and displacement contours are shown in Fig. 4.4.4 (b-c). The strain contour revealed that the max strain occurs at the joining between subcomponent to metal top frame as well as at the left metal insert location as highlighted in Fig. 4.4.5(c). These areas are further redesigned to obtain the final design shown in Fig. 4.4.6 (a). On the right side, the subcomponent is redesigned to ensure the overall weight of the component is minimized while the max. displacement is reduced at the same time. Figure 4.4.5.
